Linking Constituency Characteristics and Social Media Engagement¶

Created by Emma Jones and Maggie Parsons

Website Link: https://teragram04.github.io/

Project Plans and Dataset¶

Project Plan

With the advent of social media, humanity has never been more connected. However, with this connection comes the ability to see opinions on politics from people one has never met, in addition to providing politicians with large platforms. Using the data from Kaggle, We will analyze the link between partisanship, constituency characteristics and social media engagement, especially focusing on the proportion of partisan versus neutral messaging, and what these messages advocate for (policy changes, providing information, etc.). This work is a modern extension of the Grimmers's Appropriators not Position Takers: The Distorting Effects of Electoral Incentives on Congressional Representation, renowned in congressional research. This paper coined the term 'homestyle', which refers to the manner in which a congressman relates to his or her constituency. Here we will examine congressmans' 'digital homestyle' which accounts for both message content and message bias to get an in-depth look on the way diversity, income, and partisanship affect a politicians social media engagement.

Collaboration Plan

The students behind this paper intend to collaborate through arranging times to work through Slack. We will meet to discuss the milestone criteria, then divide the work evenly. Additionally, we will check in with each other to ensure that we stay on track for project completion.

The Dataset

The dataset we will be examining is "Political Social Media Posts", pulled from Kaggle. This dataset provides a sample of 5,000 social media posts from various politicians, and categorizes them based on a myriad of variables such as bias, intended audience, a unique id for the politician, and more. This dataset will allow us to determine which kind of message politicians use the most to garner support online- e.g., do politicans favor a national audience, or one primarily composed of their constituency?

In milestone 2, we loaded the 2015 census data from Kaggle, which is detailed below.

Now, we'll add in a dataset which matches senator names with party. This dataset was compiled by https://unitedstates.github.io/congress-legislators/ using Goverment websites.

In [ ]:
# adds current legislators
partydf = pd.read_csv('legislators-current.csv')
selected_columns = ['full_name', 'party']
partydf = partydf[selected_columns]
partydf = partydf.rename(columns={'full_name': 'legislator_Name'})
kgposts = pd.merge(kgposts, partydf, on='legislator_Name', how='left')
In [ ]:
# adds historical legislators
partydf = pd.read_csv('legislators-historical.csv')
selected_columns = ['full_name', 'party']
partydf = partydf[selected_columns]
partydf = partydf.rename(columns={'full_name': 'legislator_Name', 'party': 'party_hist'}) # Rename 'party' to 'party_hist'
kgposts = pd.merge(kgposts, partydf, on='legislator_Name', how='left')

# Update the 'party' column in kgposts with values from 'party_hist'
kgposts['party'] = kgposts['party'].fillna(kgposts['party_hist'])

# Drop the 'party_hist' column
kgposts = kgposts.drop(columns=['party_hist'])

Meanwhile, _trusted_judgements can remain an integer, as we could perform quantitative operations to determine outcomes (e.g, what is the average number of _trusted_judgrments per post?) The rest of the variables appear to be the correct type.

Summary Statistics¶

Now that the data is correctly loaded and has the correct dtypes, let's do some basic analysis! The first question we are asking is what is the most common type of message politicians aim to deliver? This dataset divides the messages into nine categories: attack, constituency, information, media, mobilization, other, personal, policy, and support. Let's count up how many of each message appear throughout the dataset.

In [ ]:
message_type_count = kgposts.message.value_counts()
message_type_count
Out[ ]:
count
message
policy 1411
personal 1170
support 921
information 647
media 277
attack 172
constituency 152
mobilization 129
other 121

It looks politicians primarily use their platforms to discuss policy! Surprisingly, attack messages come in 6th place, despite how hostile politics on social media can feel. Let's make a graph so we have a visual of the message variety and count.

In [ ]:
kgposts.message.value_counts().plot.bar()
Out[ ]:
<Axes: xlabel='message'>

So now we know which type of message is the most popular, but what about the platform they're posted on? Let's use the same process to determine which platform appears to be the most popular.

In [ ]:
platform_type_count = kgposts.source.value_counts()
platform_type_count
Out[ ]:
count
source
twitter 2500
facebook 2500

In this case, it looks like it is split perfectly in half! (the dataset contains 5,000 total posts). This was likely done purposefully during data collection. However, this raises a new question; although policy messages are the most popular overall, does this change across platforms? Let's find out!

In [ ]:

This turned out to be quite a lengthy process, so we did it in a seperate notebook and turned it into a csv which was then uploaded to the github.

In [ ]:
'''partydf2 = pd.read_csv('fixedfinalmissingleg.csv')

partydf2 = partydf2.rename(columns={'Name': 'legislator_Name'})
kgposts = pd.merge(kgposts, partydf, on='legislator_Name', how='left')'''

# Load partydf2
partydf2 = pd.read_csv('fixedfinalmissingleg.csv')
partydf2 = partydf2.rename(columns={'Name': 'legislator_Name'})

# Clean legislator names in both DataFrames
kgposts['legislator_Name'] = kgposts['legislator_Name'].str.strip()  # Remove leading/trailing spaces
partydf2['legislator_Name'] = partydf2['legislator_Name'].str.strip()

# Merge on cleaned names using 'left' join to keep all kgposts rows
kgposts = pd.merge(kgposts, partydf2[['legislator_Name', 'Party']], on='legislator_Name', how='left')

# Update 'party' column with values from 'Party'
kgposts['party'] = kgposts['party'].fillna(kgposts['Party'])

# Drop the temporary 'Party' column
kgposts = kgposts.drop(columns=['Party'])

kgposts.head()

This looks like a good overview, but there are some issues we need to address. Going forward, we want to examine this data on a statewide basis, not a county-wide one. To address this, let's create a new dataframe that will include either the summation or the average of the values we want to study to get a picture of an entire state's makeup.

In [ ]:
#Create a new dataframe that looks at the census info on a state-wide basis.
#Sum the integers and average the percentages

Census_Data_Statewide = census_data_2015.groupby('State').apply(lambda x: pd.Series({
    'TotalPop': x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Hispanic': (x['Hispanic'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'White': (x['White'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Black': (x['Black'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Native': (x['Native'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Asian': (x['Asian'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Pacific': (x['Pacific'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Men': x['Men'].sum(),
    'Women': x['Women'].sum(),
    'PublicWork': (x['PublicWork'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'PrivateWork': (x['PrivateWork'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'IncomePerCap': (x['IncomePerCap'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum(),
    'Income': (x['Income'] * x['TotalPop']).sum() / x['TotalPop'].sum()
}))

Now that we have this breakdown, let's move onto our questions!

Question 1: Does a state's high diversity affect how a senator phrases his social media post?¶

It was generally understood in the field of Congressional Literature that the political makeup of a district ie. how divided the constituency, has an impact on the how a Senator will communicate with his or her district. When this work was conducted using Senate data from 2006 to 2008, press releases where the predominant form of social media. Today, twitter posts are vying for that position. We compare census data by states against senators because the entire state votes on both senators. We will compare below the association between diversity and homestyle, meaning whether a senator relates to their district in terms of attack messages, support messages, policy messages etc. Note that bias is also a factor in homestyle, which will be explored in later questions.

Our first question is fairly self-explanatory: Does a state's diversity affect how senators feel they should word their social media posts? We decided to use the US Census Bureau's "Racial and Ethnic Diversity in the United States: 2010 Census and 2020 Census" page to determine which states are the most diverse, and which are the least.

**In 2010, the top 5 most racially diverse states were***

  1. Hawaii
  2. California
  3. Texas
  4. Nevada
  5. New Mexico

*Wahsington D.C. ranked #5 but because it has no represenation in the senate we left it off the list

Let's take these states and put them in a separate dataframe

Interesting! It looks like diverse states tend to send mostly support and policy messages (they make up around 2/3 of the total messages!) So to answer question one...

Q1: Senators representing diverse states prefer to send support and policy messages

Question 2: Does a state's low diversity affect how a senator phrases his social media post?¶

Well, since we've examined the most diverse states, why not examine the least diverse states as well to see if the message type differs. According to the website we used in Question 1, the five least racially diverse states in 2010 are *

  1. Maine
  2. Vermont
  3. New Hampshire
  4. North Dakota
  5. Montana*

*The true number 3 on this list, West Virginia, had no social media posts, so we moved down the list to the next state that had social media posts (Montana).

Now, we will repeat the same process as above for these states, so feel free to move down to the results if you'd like.

Interesting! Like high diversity states, politicians sent mostly support and policy messages. Policy messages make up 29% of the low diversity state messages, and 36% of the high diversity state messages.

The big difference comes from the number of information and personal messages being sent. These messages made up 8% and 17.5% respectively of the total messages sent for the high diversity states. For the low diversity states, they made up 18% each for a total of 36% of the messages.

To conclude: Q3: Senators representing non-diverse states also prefer to send support and policy messages, but send significantly more information messages as well.

Question 3: Does a state's high diversity affect a senator's perceived bias in social media posts?¶

The Kaggle dataset described social media posts in one of two ways: partisan or neutral. Partisan means that the politician's posts aligned with his/her political party, while neutral means they did not necesarily post along party lines. This question aims to examine whether states with a diverse population have senators that post more partisan or more neutral social media messages.

To begin, we'll call on our old friend, diverse_states_df

We find the states with the lowest income per capita are: Mississipi, Arkansas, Idaho, West Virginia, and New Mexico. Missisipi and WV aren't in the kaggle data set so we'll go to 6th and 7th place.

# Create a figure and two subplots
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))  # 1 row, 2 columns

# Plot the first bar chart on the first subplot (ax1) - High Income
value_sums_3.plot.bar(x='MessageType', y='Number', ax=ax1)
ax1.set_title('High Income States')
ax1.set_ylim(0, 40)  # Set y-axis limit to 40


value_sums_4.plot.bar(x='MessageType', y='Number', ax=ax2)
ax2.set_title('Low Income States')
ax2.set_ylim(0, 40)  # Set y-axis limit to 40

# Adjust spacing between subplots
plt.tight_layout()

# Display the plot
plt.show()

It seems that income may not closely correlate with message types. Something of note, however is the proportion of policy messages in low income states is higher than those in high income states.

Future Plans:¶

We plan to examine the correlation between diversity, income or public/private work and frequency of bias. We will also examine the same factors against message types.

We will then examine the connection of party and message style, frequency of bias. In the end we will be able to determine the association between demographic factors and senators' digital homestyles. We will be able to further understand whether party membership plays a role in this relationship.
